description: Master graph representations (Adjacency Matrix, Adjacency List, Edge List), Breadth-First Search (BFS), Depth-First Search (DFS), Connected Components, Cycle Detection in directed & undirected graphs, Bipartite Graphs (2-coloring), Kahn's Topological Sorting algorithm, Kosaraju's and Tarjan's Strongly Connected Components (SCC), Bridges, and Articulation Points.

scenarios.title: Optimizing Social Network Friend-of-Friend Recommendations
scenarios.description: A social network with 100 million users needs to compute degree-of-separation paths and 2nd-degree friend suggestions with minimal latency and memory overhead.
scenarios.solution: Represent the social network as an Adjacency List (Map<Integer, Set<Integer>> or IntArrayList) since friendship is sparse. Run multi-source level-limited BFS with a visited BitSet to find 2-hop neighbors in O(k²) time where k is average degree, without allocating full V arrays.

scenarios.title: Automated Build System Dependency Resolver
scenarios.description: A continuous integration pipeline has 5,000 microservice build targets with interdependent compilation constraints and must schedule builds in parallel while catching circular dependencies immediately.
scenarios.solution: Model microservice build targets as vertices in a DAG with directed edges u -> v meaning target u must compile before target v. Run Kahn's Algorithm using an in-degree array. If the number of processed tasks is less than 5,000, report circular dependency deadlock; otherwise dispatch zero in-degree tasks concurrently.

scenarios.title: Critical Telecommunication Fiber Line Failure Analysis
scenarios.description: A national optical internet provider needs to identify single points of failure (lines whose disconnection divides the network into disjoint isolated islands).
scenarios.solution: Run Tarjan's Bridge-Finding DFS algorithm using discovery times disc[] and low-link values low[]. Any edge (u, v) satisfying low[v] > disc[u] is a critical bridge. Re-routing redundancy must be added across all identified bridge edges.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about graph representations is correct for a sparse graph with V = 100,000 vertices and E = 200,000 edges?
options: Adjacency Matrix requires O(V) space and enables O(1) neighbor iteration.
Adjacency Matrix requires O(V²) space (~40 GB of RAM) whereas Adjacency List requires O(V + E) space.
Edge List allows querying whether an edge (u, v) exists in O(1) time.
Adjacency List requires more memory than Adjacency Matrix when E << V².
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix of size 100,000 x 100,000 contains 10^10 integer cells (~40 GB). An adjacency list only stores the actual edges (200,000 entries), requiring O(V + E) auxiliary space, which easily fits in a few megabytes.

questions.question: In an undirected graph with V vertices and E edges, what is the sum of degrees of all vertices according to the Handshaking Lemma?
options: E
questions.explanation: By the Handshaking Lemma, every undirected edge connects two endpoints and contributes exactly 1 to the degree of both endpoints. Therefore, the sum of degrees of all vertices equals 2 * E.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS) on a graph represented using an Adjacency List?
options: O(V²)
O(V * E)
O(V + E)
O(V log E)
questions.explanation: Using an adjacency list, every vertex is enqueued/visited once (O(V)), and each edge is inspected from its endpoints once in directed or twice in undirected graphs (O(E)). Total time complexity is O(V + E).

questions.question: Why does BFS always find the shortest path in terms of number of edges in an unweighted graph, whereas DFS cannot guarantee it?
options: BFS explores nodes level by level using a FIFO Queue, visiting all distance-d nodes before any distance-(d+1) node.
BFS uses a PriorityQueue sorted by edge weights.
DFS uses recursion which skips cycles.
BFS iterates over nodes in sorted numerical order.
questions.explanation: BFS explores nodes in strict non-decreasing order of hop distance from the start node using a FIFO queue. The first time a target vertex is reached, the path length is guaranteed to be minimal. DFS plunges deep along one path and may find a much longer route.

questions.question: How can you detect a cycle in an UNDIRECTED graph during DFS traversal?
options: If a neighbor is already visited and is NOT the immediate parent vertex.
If a neighbor is already visited regardless of whether it is the parent.
If all neighbors of a vertex have in-degree greater than 1.
If the call stack depth exceeds the number of edges.
questions.explanation: In an undirected graph, the edge back to the immediate parent is the edge we just traversed. If we encounter a visited neighbor that is NOT our parent, an alternate path back to that ancestor exists, confirming a cycle.

questions.question: Why can the undirected cycle detection condition (visited[neighbor] && neighbor != parent) NOT be used directly for DIRECTED graphs?
options: Directed graphs cannot have cycles.
Two directed edges converging onto a common child (cross edge) would be falsely flagged as a cycle.
Directed graphs do not support visited arrays.
Directed graphs only allow BFS, not DFS.
questions.explanation: In a directed graph, two independent paths can converge onto the same node (e.g. 1 -> 3 and 2 -> 3). Vertex 3 is visited from 1, and when reached from 2, it is already visited but does NOT form a directed cycle (it is a cross edge). Cycle detection in directed graphs requires tracking the active recursion stack (Back Edges).

questions.question: In the 3-state coloring algorithm for cycle detection in directed graphs (0 = Unvisited, 1 = Visiting / in call stack, 2 = Fully processed), what condition indicates a cycle?
options: Encountering a neighbor with state 0.
Encountering a neighbor with state 2.
Encountering a neighbor with state 1 (Back Edge).
Encountering a leaf vertex with no outgoing edges.
questions.explanation: State 1 represents vertices currently on the active recursion call stack. If an edge leads to a neighbor currently in state 1, it forms a Back Edge to an ancestor, confirming a directed cycle.

questions.question: A graph is bipartite if and only if:
options: It contains no cycles of odd length.
It is a complete graph.
Every vertex has an even degree.
It is strongly connected.
questions.explanation: By Konig's Theorem, a graph is bipartite (2-colorable) if and only if it contains no odd-length cycles. If an odd-length cycle exists, trying to alternate colors will inevitably result in adjacent vertices having the same color.

questions.question: What is a prerequisite condition for a graph to have a valid Topological Ordering?
options: The graph must be undirected and connected.
The graph must be a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
The graph must contain at least one Hamiltonian cycle.
The graph must have equal in-degrees and out-degrees.
questions.explanation: Topological sorting linearly orders vertices such that for every directed edge u -> v, u appears before v. If the graph contains a directed cycle (e.g., A -> B -> A), no valid ordering can place A before B and B before A simultaneously. Thus, only DAGs have topological orderings.

questions.question: How does Kahn's algorithm for Topological Sort detect whether a directed graph contains a cycle?
options: By checking if any vertex has in-degree of 0.
By comparing the count of vertices popped from the queue with total vertices V: if count < V, a cycle exists.
By counting the number of edges visited.
By maintaining an ancestor pointer for each node.
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly enqueues and removes vertices with in-degree 0. Nodes trapped in a directed cycle never reach an in-degree of 0. If the total number of removed vertices is less than V, the remaining vertices form cycles.

questions.question: What is a Strongly Connected Component (SCC) in a directed graph?
options: A maximal subset of vertices where every vertex is reachable from every other vertex in the subset.
A group of vertices connected by undirected bridges.
A subset of vertices whose degrees sum to 2E.
A spanning tree with minimal total edge weight.
questions.explanation: In a directed graph, an SCC is a maximal subgraph such that for every pair of vertices u and v, there exists a directed path from u to v and from v to u.

questions.question: Why does Kosaraju's Algorithm reverse (transpose) all edges of the directed graph in Step 2?
options: To convert the directed graph into an undirected graph.
To prevent DFS from escaping the current SCC into already processed sink SCCs when traversing in reverse finish-time order.
To reduce the space complexity from O(V+E) to O(V).
To eliminate self-loops and parallel edges.
questions.explanation: Reversing the graph turns SCC sources into SCC sinks. By running DFS on the transposed graph in decreasing order of original finish times, DFS is confined strictly within each individual SCC without leaking into neighboring SCCs.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Kosaraju's algorithm vs Tarjan's SCC algorithm?
options: Kosaraju is O(V³) while Tarjan is O(V²).
Both are O(V + E) time, but Tarjan requires only a single DFS pass whereas Kosaraju requires two DFS passes and graph transposition.
Tarjan is O(V log V) while Kosaraju is O(V + E).
Kosaraju works on weighted graphs whereas Tarjan works only on unweighted graphs.
questions.explanation: Both algorithms achieve linear O(V + E) time. Kosaraju runs two DFS passes (first for finish-time stack, second on transposed graph), whereas Tarjan finds all SCCs in a single DFS pass using discovery times and low-link values.

questions.question: In Tarjan's Bridge-Finding algorithm, an edge (u, v) in a DFS tree is identified as a bridge (critical connection) if and only if:
options: low[v] < disc[u]
low[v] == disc[u]
low[v] > disc[u]
low[u] == disc[v]
questions.explanation: The condition low[v] > disc[u] means that from subtree v and its descendants, the lowest discovery time reachable via back-edges is strictly greater than disc[u]. Thus, v has no back-edge to u or any ancestor of u; removing (u, v) disconnects the graph.

questions.question: In Tarjan's Articulation Point algorithm, what are the conditions for a vertex u to be an articulation point (cut vertex)?
options: If u is the DFS tree root with >= 2 children, OR if u is not the root and has a child v such that low[v] >= disc[u].
If u has an odd degree.
If low[u] == 0 for all neighbors.
If u has in-degree == out-degree.
questions.explanation: The root of a DFS tree is a cut vertex if and only if it has at least 2 independent subtrees in the DFS tree. A non-root vertex u is a cut vertex if it has a child v such that low[v] >= disc[u], meaning v has no back-edge reaching an ancestor above u.

questions.question: What subtle bug occurs when running BFS or DFS on a disconnected graph if you only start from vertex 0?
options: It throws a NullPointerException.
It fails to visit vertices in disconnected components, leading to incomplete traversals or missed cycles.
It enters an infinite recursion.
It causes memory overflow.
questions.explanation: If a graph contains multiple components (or unreachable nodes in directed graphs), starting traversal only from node 0 will never reach nodes in other components. You must wrap the traversal in an outer loop: for (int i = 0; i < V; i++) if (!visited[i]) traverse(i);

questions.question: When should you use multi-source BFS instead of single-source BFS?
options: When finding shortest paths from multiple simultaneous origins (e.g. 01 Matrix, Rotten Oranges, Wall and Gates).
When the graph has negative edge weights.
When finding Strongly Connected Components in directed graphs.
When detecting cycles in DAGs.
questions.explanation: Multi-source BFS initializes the queue with all source nodes simultaneously at distance 0 (e.g., all rotten oranges or all 0s in a grid), expanding wavefronts outward in lockstep to find minimum distances to any source in O(V + E) total time.

questions.question: Why is an Edge List representation inefficient for neighbor traversal operations in algorithms like BFS and DFS?
options: Edge lists cannot store vertex labels.
Finding all neighbors of a single vertex u requires scanning all E edges, making full graph traversal O(V * E) instead of O(V + E).
Edge lists cannot handle undirected edges.
Edge lists require O(V²) memory.
questions.explanation: In an edge list, edges are stored in an unsorted list. To inspect the outgoing edges of vertex u, one must iterate through the entire list of E edges. Repeating this for all V vertices yields an inefficient O(V * E) runtime.

questions.question: In Tarjan's SCC algorithm, why do we update low[u] = Math.min(low[u], disc[v]) for a back-edge (u, v) instead of low[v]?
options: Because v is already in low[u].
Because low[v] might reflect a back-edge to a node outside the current strongly connected component.
Because disc[v] is always greater than low[v].
To avoid division by zero in recursion.
questions.explanation: A back edge from u to v points directly to an ancestor v. Using low[v] could inadvertently reach an ancestor that belongs to a different SCC through an earlier cross-edge. Using disc[v] strictly limits the reachability calculation to direct back-edges within the active component.

questions.question: Which algorithm should you choose to find the shortest path between two vertices in an unweighted grid with obstacles?
options: Dijkstra's Algorithm with a Min-Heap
Breadth-First Search (BFS)
Depth-First Search (DFS)
Kosaraju's Algorithm
questions.explanation: In an unweighted grid, every step costs 1. BFS finds the shortest path in linear O(R * C) time with minimal overhead using a simple queue, whereas Dijkstra adds unnecessary heap overhead O(R * C log(R*C)), and DFS does not guarantee the shortest path.
